description:
​Ben Yasemin; özellikle uzay temalı konularda derinlemesine araştırma yapma ve bu bilgileri fonksiyonel bir tasarıma dönüştürme konusunda büyük bir ilgi ve tutkuya sahibim. Bu süreçte hem araştıran hem de üreten dinamik bir ekiple birlikte çalışmayı hedefliyorum.
  
​Ekibime katılacak; araştırmacı ruhu olan, tasarım odaklı düşünen ya da bu alanda birlikte yol almak isteyen saygılı ve yenilikçi takım arkadaşları arıyorum.
summary:
One of humanity's greatest goals in space exploration is to establish permanent crewed bases on the Moon and Mars. However, planetary surfaces pose severe risks for open habitats due to extreme temperature fluctuations, micrometeorites, and lethal cosmic radiation.

The foundation of our project is the scientific pilot model officially validated by NASA prior to the Mars 2020 Perseverance mission. According to NASA Earth Observatory and Mars Exploration Program data, Lake Salda in Turkey is the highest-fidelity terrestrial analog to Mars' Jezero Crater in terms of magnesium carbonate mineralogy and ancient lakebed structure.

We take this existing "lakebed and biosignature" model one step further. Rather than focusing on open surface basins, we developed a brand-new set of analogies targeting underground volcanic structures and lava tubes for permanent bases on both Mars and the Moon. Specifically, we pair Kula Volcanic Geopark with lunar and Martian lava tubes, and Cappadocia's underground cities with Mars' volcanic tuff deposits. By analyzing these sites through Thermal Stability, Mechanical Strength, and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), our project transforms Turkey’s volcanic heritage into a vital testing ground for future subterranean space habitats.
details:
Our project is a terrestrial-to-space subterranean analog mapping and suitability analysis framework developed to enable humanity to build permanent, safe, and sustainable habitats on the Moon and Mars. Our work is grounded in the Lake Salda and Jezero Crater pilot model, which was scientifically validated by NASA prior to the Mars 2020 Perseverance mission. While NASA’s pairing focused on magnesium carbonate mineralogy and ancient lakebed data to search for past microbial biosignatures, our project adopts this proven methodology and introduces a fundamental paradigm shift: rather than focusing on open surface crater basins, we target subterranean volcanic structures, lava tubes, and volcanic tuff formations that are critical for future crewed colonization. Our system operates through a three-stage methodology: First, satellite imagery, topographic maps, and mineralogical datasets obtained from NASA Earth Observatory, NASA Worldview, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) platforms are integrated with terrestrial geological field data from Turkey. Second, the selected Earth sites and space targets are analyzed across three core engineering criteria: thermal stability and insulation, structural integrity and rock mechanics strength, and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU). Third, analog matching and calibration are performed; within this scope, the Kula Volcanic Geopark in Manisa is paired with the Arsia Mons pit craters on Mars and the Marius Hills lava tubes on the Moon to evaluate basaltic roof strength and construction material conversion potential, while the underground cities of Cappadocia in Nevşehir are paired with the Medusae Fossae Formation—massive volcanic ash deposits near the Martian equator—and modeled using centuries-proven subterranean climate control and thermal equilibrium data.

The benefits and intended impact of this work are substantial. Considering the astronomical cost of launching every kilogram of payload into space, utilizing a planet's natural geological cavities instead of transporting heavy radiation shielding from Earth dramatically reduces mission costs. Furthermore, subterranean lava tubes and tuff formations act as a natural shield against extreme day-night thermal shocks, micrometeorite impacts, and cosmic radiation, thereby maximizing astronaut safety and transforming Turkey’s unique volcanic geoparks into standardized analog testing centers for international space agencies.

The most creative and original aspect of our project is that, unlike the majority of existing space analog studies confined to surface desert or crater environments, it bridges one of humanity’s oldest subterranean engineering heritages—the underground cities of Cappadocia—and young basaltic volcanism with cutting-edge space-age settlement technologies. Instead of merely replicating NASA’s established Salda-Jezero methodology, we transform this model from an exploratory tool searching for the past into an architectural and engineering matrix building for the future, offering a novel perspective to the literature and establishing a dual-target analog framework applicable to both the Moon and Mars rather than limiting our scope to a single celestial body. Throughout the development process, open-data portals from NASA, Worldview and MRO HiRISE archives, Google Earth Pro, and spatial comparison tools were utilized, while our team also accounted for practical constraints encountered in real space missions beyond theoretical similarities. Accordingly, multi-date satellite layers were screened to overcome atmospheric obstacles such as cloud cover, thermal stability and natural ventilation shaft architecture vital for long-duration astronaut stays were prioritized, and the in-situ workability of local rocks was established as a core selection criterion to ensure a self-sustaining base.
